title: CPU Utilization Trending (Windows)
exclusions: Measures host-wide busy time from the Windows PDH path `\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` as percentage points from 0 through 100. It does not measure processor frequency-adjusted utility, per-process consumption, per-core imbalance, processor queue length, DPC/interrupt attribution, application latency, guest-versus-hypervisor contention, or root cause. Task Manager on current Windows can use `Processor Information\% Processor Utility`, so its display is not a same-counter oracle and can exceed 100 under Turbo Boost while this counter must not. The primary SPL covers only `mode=single` event-index data with `source=sourcetype=Perfmon:CPU`; `PerfmonMk:CPU`, `PerfmonMetrics:CPU`, metric indexes, WMI, OpenTelemetry, and other collectors require separately tested searches. The 90-percent threshold, three five-minute bucket policy, 80-percent recovery level, delayed search window, sample-coverage minimum, and exception scope are deployment policy—not Microsoft or Splunk universal defaults. A result establishes sustained aggregate busy time under that policy; it does not prove a CPU bottleneck, capacity shortage, defective process, attack, or regulatory condition. Missing, late, duplicate, nonnumeric, out-of-range, wrong-instance, wrong-counter, or under-covered telemetry is a source-health defect and must not be interpreted as low CPU.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows package/version and compatibility record; deployment-app `local/inputs.conf`; effective `btool inputs list CPU --debug` output; Windows/forwarder/search-platform versions; expected-host inventory; one raw `Perfmon:CPU` event proving object, counter, instance, value, timestamp, source, and source type; the `windows_cpu_utilization_trending` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch window/history, and exported result rows; independent telemetry-health results for missing, late, duplicate, invalid, or under-covered samples; dashboard and alert-action revisions; threshold and recovery approval; bounded exception records; incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, boundary, gap, duplicate, and recovery control outputs. Result evidence must preserve host, first/last qualified bucket, bucket/sample counts, sustained average, minimum and peak, threshold, persistence, and indexing time. This documentation-only review created no Windows, PDH, forwarder, CIM-acceleration, saved-search, alert, or production evidence and does not prove runtime compatibility or control effectiveness.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated event index and absolute test window matching the SPL's 15-minute closed interval, ingest `source=Perfmon:CPU sourcetype=Perfmon:CPU` events for `host=win-cpu-positive`, `object=Processor`, `counter=% Processor Time`, and `instance=_Total`. Provide ten unique, numeric 30-second samples in each of three consecutive five-minute buckets; make each bucket average 92.0 percentage points, keep every value within 0..100, and place indexing times before dispatch. Expect exactly one result with `qualified_buckets=3`, `high_buckets=3`, `sample_count=30`, `persistence_minutes=15`, `threshold_pct=90`, `sustained_avg_cpu_pct=92`, and first/last bucket epochs 600 seconds apart.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero primary alert rows for each: only two high buckets; three buckets averaging 89.99; high/low/high buckets; one bucket with fewer than eight samples; one bucket whose first-to-last accepted sample spans less than 210 seconds; nonconsecutive bucket starts; `instance=0` instead of `_Total`; `object=Processor Information`; `% Processor Utility` or `% Idle Time`; `PerfmonMk:CPU`; nonnumeric, negative, or greater-than-100 `Value`; and duplicate raw events sharing host and exact sample time. Boundary tests must accept exactly 90.0 and reject 89.99. A separate recovery test should require three qualified consecutive bucket averages below 80 before closing an incident; exception testing must suppress notification only for an exact host and bounded epoch interval while preserving the base result and telemetry-health evidence.

dataSources: Primary authority: Windows Performance Data Helper counter `\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time`, collected locally every 30 seconds by the Splunk platform Perfmon input configured through Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows stanza `[perfmon://CPU]`. This implementation pins `object=Processor`, `counters=% Processor Time`, `instances=_Total`, `useEnglishOnly=true`, `mode=single`, `index=perfmon`, yielding event data with `source=Perfmon:CPU`, `sourcetype=Perfmon:CPU`, and fields `collection`, `object`, `counter`, `instance`, `Value`, `host`, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Optional normalized source: the add-on maps `Perfmon:CPU` to CIM Performance/CPU, including `cpu_load_percent` and destination identity. Optional metric-index collection uses `mode=single` with a metrics index and metric name `Processor.%_Processor_Time`, but requires `mstats` and is not searched by the primary SPL.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), with the collection component on each Windows Universal Forwarder and the release's parsing/search-time knowledge on the Splunk tiers required by the deployment topology. Use a currently supported add-on/platform combination and test upgrades; the add-on is not the Universal Forwarder itself. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=perfmon source="Perfmon:CPU" sourcetype="Perfmon:CPU" object="Processor" counter="% Processor Time" instance="_Total" earliest=-25m@m latest=-10m@m
| eval cpu_pct=tonumber(Value), sample_epoch=_time, valid_value=if(isnotnull(cpu_pct) AND cpu_pct>=0 AND cpu_pct<=100,1,0)
| stats count AS raw_event_count sum(valid_value) AS valid_event_count avg(cpu_pct) AS cpu_pct max(_indextime) AS last_indextime by host _time
| where raw_event_count=1 AND valid_event_count=1
| eval sample_epoch=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS sample_count avg(cpu_pct) AS avg_cpu_pct min(cpu_pct) AS min_cpu_pct max(cpu_pct) AS peak_cpu_pct min(sample_epoch) AS first_sample_epoch max(sample_epoch) AS last_sample_epoch max(last_indextime) AS last_indextime by host _time
| eval sample_span_seconds=last_sample_epoch-first_sample_epoch
| where sample_count>=8 AND sample_count<=12 AND sample_span_seconds>=210
| eval bucket_over_threshold=if(avg_cpu_pct>=90,1,0)
| stats count AS qualified_buckets sum(bucket_over_threshold) AS high_buckets sum(sample_count) AS sample_count avg(avg_cpu_pct) AS sustained_avg_cpu_pct min(min_cpu_pct) AS minimum_cpu_pct max(peak_cpu_pct) AS peak_cpu_pct min(_time) AS first_bucket_epoch max(_time) AS last_bucket_epoch max(last_indextime) AS last_indextime by host
| where qualified_buckets=3 AND high_buckets=3 AND last_bucket_epoch-first_bucket_epoch=600
| eval sustained_avg_cpu_pct=round(sustained_avg_cpu_pct,2), minimum_cpu_pct=round(minimum_cpu_pct,2), peak_cpu_pct=round(peak_cpu_pct,2), threshold_pct=90, persistence_minutes=15, recovery_pct=80, use_case="UC-1.2.1"
| table host sustained_avg_cpu_pct minimum_cpu_pct peak_cpu_pct threshold_pct persistence_minutes recovery_pct qualified_buckets high_buckets sample_count first_bucket_epoch last_bucket_epoch last_indextime use_case
| sort 0 -sustained_avg_cpu_pct host
description: Detects Windows hosts whose aggregate `Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` averages at least 90 percentage points in each of three consecutive, adequately sampled five-minute buckets. The rule rejects wrong counters and instances, duplicate timestamps, invalid values, sparse buckets, and nonconsecutive persistence before returning a host.
value: Sustained fleet-level CPU saturation can delay application work, increase request latency, and leave little headroom for bursts or failover. A closed-bucket, coverage-aware trend helps Windows operations reduce false pages from ordinary short spikes, shorten diagnosis, and plan capacity without confusing frequency-adjusted utility with processor busy time.
implementation: Install a supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows release on the required Windows collection and Splunk knowledge tiers. Enable a local `[perfmon://CPU]` input for `Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` at 30-second cadence in `mode=single` to an event index, verify the exact source/fields and 0..100 unit contract, then save `windows_cpu_utilization_trending`. Run every five minutes against three fully closed five-minute buckets delayed for indexing; page at three bucket averages >=90, recover only after three qualified buckets <80, and operate telemetry health separately.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — CPU Utilization Trending`: top row shows expected hosts missing qualified recent data, rejected/duplicate sample counts, hosts currently in the 15-minute high state, and fleet p95 aggregate busy time. Plot a 24-hour line per selected host from valid `_Total` samples with 80% recovery and 90% alert reference bands; overlay bucket sample counts or mark under-covered buckets rather than drawing them as zero. Add a heat map of host by five-minute bucket using average percentage points, and a sortable incident table with sustained average, minimum, peak, sample count, first/last bucket, owner, and exception state. Drill down to raw Perfmon events, per-logical-processor `Processor` instances, `System\Processor Queue Length`, `% User Time`, `% Privileged Time`, `% DPC Time`, `% Interrupt Time`, Process/Process V2 telemetry, Task Manager/Perfmon, change records, and application latency. Do not mix `% Processor Utility`, process percentages, or metric-index series into the same axis without explicit labels.
schema: Windows PDH Processor(_Total) busy-time percentage; normalized context in CIM Performance/All_Performance/CPU
cimSpl:
| tstats summariesonly=t avg(All_Performance.CPU.cpu_load_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct count AS normalized_event_count from datamodel=Performance.All_Performance where nodename=All_Performance.CPU by _time span=5m All_Performance.dest
| rename All_Performance.dest AS host
| where isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(avg_cpu_pct) AND avg_cpu_pct>=0 AND avg_cpu_pct<=100
| eval bucket_over_threshold=if(avg_cpu_pct>=90,1,0)
| stats count AS qualified_buckets sum(bucket_over_threshold) AS high_buckets sum(normalized_event_count) AS normalized_event_count avg(avg_cpu_pct) AS sustained_avg_cpu_pct min(_time) AS first_bucket_epoch max(_time) AS last_bucket_epoch by host
| where qualified_buckets=3 AND high_buckets=3 AND last_bucket_epoch-first_bucket_epoch=600
| eval sustained_avg_cpu_pct=round(sustained_avg_cpu_pct,2), threshold_pct=90, persistence_minutes=15, use_case="UC-1.2.1-cim-trend"

| sort 0 -sustained_avg_cpu_pct host
dataModelAcceleration: Optional, not the primary alert authority. The add-on documents `Perfmon:CPU` mapping to CIM Performance, and CIM defines `All_Performance.CPU.cpu_load_percent` plus destination identity. Before enabling the alternative `tstats` trend, validate the installed add-on's event type/tags/field aliases, destination parity, value units, source population, acceleration coverage, and generated Pivot search. Standard CIM does not preserve this rule's `object`, `counter`, `_Total` instance, raw `Value`, exact 30-second cadence, duplicate identity, or per-bucket coverage contract; other tagged CPU sources can enter the same dataset. Therefore the CIM search is normalized trend/corroboration only and must not silently replace the raw-event persistence rule. `summariesonly=t` intentionally returns no data when summaries are incomplete; monitor acceleration health separately.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row means three qualified five-minute averages really met the configured 90-percent policy. “False positive” therefore means the load was authorized or the policy/scope was unsuitable—not that Splunk invented CPU time.

1. **Approved patching and servicing** — Windows Update, component servicing, .NET native-image work, Defender post-update scans, and installer custom actions can sustain aggregate busy time. Correlate exact host, KB/package, maintenance ticket, `WinEventLog:System`, Windows Update logs, process evidence, and recovery after the window. Do not create a permanent Patch Tuesday exclusion.

2. **Defender, EDR, backup, inventory, or vulnerability scan** — Security and management agents can legitimately consume CPU for longer than 15 minutes. Confirm the named process/service, scan job, policy, owner, expected duration, application latency, and completion. Repeated customer impact remains a scheduling/capacity problem even when the process is authorized.

3. **Batch, build, reporting, index maintenance, or media workload** — Scheduled computation can be intentionally CPU-bound. Match the workload run ID and service objective, compare queue/latency and completion time, then route to the workload owner or capacity review instead of globally suppressing the server class.

4. **Failover, cold cache, application start, or traffic surge** — Service recovery can move work to fewer hosts and sustain CPU while caches compile or warm. Correlate load balancer membership, restart/failover events, request rate, error rate, queue length, and peer-host headroom. An expected cause does not make a breached recovery objective harmless.

5. **Virtual-machine host contention or power policy** — The guest can report high busy time while effective work is constrained by hypervisor scheduling, frequency state, or an unsuitable power plan. Correlate hypervisor ready/steal-equivalent telemetry, host pressure, guest clock/frequency utility, and migration records; this counter alone cannot locate the bottleneck.

6. **Per-core hotspot hidden by `_Total`** — The aggregate can reach policy during a legitimate single-threaded or affinity-bound workload, or remain below policy while one logical processor is saturated. Review individual `Processor` instances and application latency. Do not change the aggregate result into a per-core diagnosis.

7. **Counter/display mismatch** — Modern Task Manager can represent frequency-adjusted Processor Utility, whereas this UC uses time-based Processor Time. Turbo Boost, throttling, and sampling intervals can make displays differ. Compare the exact `Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` counter in Windows Performance Monitor, not a visually similar CPU tile.

8. **Canary, burn-in, resilience, or synthetic load test** — Approved qualification can intentionally hold CPU above 90. Preserve it as control evidence and use a bounded exception keyed to the exact host and test interval; never suppress telemetry-health failures or unrelated hosts.

9. **Identity collision or duplicate collection** — Cloned `host` metadata, two enabled `[perfmon://CPU]` authorities, replay, or overlapping deployment apps can alter sample density. The SPL rejects exact duplicate timestamps and over-dense buckets, but near-duplicate timestamps may still look valid. Compare forwarder GUID, deployment client, effective stanza, raw timestamps, and expected-host inventory, then repair collection.

**Safe suppression:** keep the base result and source-health searches unchanged. Apply notification suppression only in a post-detection lookup against `windows_cpu_exceptions.csv`, keyed by exact `host` and `policy_id`, numeric inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, host groups, open-ended dates, expired rows, and exceptions for missing/invalid/duplicate data. Recovery is three qualified consecutive five-minute averages below 80; values from 80 through less than 90 retain the incident without repaging, providing explicit hysteresis.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites, unit, and authority

Assign a Windows platform owner, Splunk collection owner, saved-search owner, service/capacity escalation path, and telemetry-health responder. Select a Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows release that its current compatibility listing supports on the deployed Splunk Enterprise or Cloud version, and qualify the exact add-on, Universal Forwarder, Windows build, processor architecture, search tier, and CIM package in non-production. The catalogue's `splunkVersions` values describe the intended search-platform families, not proof that every add-on release supports every token. This review did not execute any combination.

Install `Splunk_TA_windows` on each Windows Universal Forwarder used for local PDH collection. Install its parsing and search-time knowledge on the tiers required by the documented deployment topology; in distributed environments that usually means the relevant parsing tier and search heads as well as collection code on forwarders. The add-on and Universal Forwarder are different products. Use deployment apps and `local` configuration, never edit the add-on's `default` directory. The forwarder service must be able to query local Windows performance counters and forward data; the search role needs read access to `index=perfmon` and permission to schedule the saved search. Keep deployment administration, alert-action administration, and incident-response privileges separate. No remote administrative share, WMI remote collection, process dump, debugger, service restart, or premium app permission is needed for the base signal.

Define the signal exactly as Windows `\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time`. Microsoft documents this as average processor usage across all logical processors, from 0 through 100 percentage points: a two-processor host with one processor busy and one idle reports 50. It is a PDH formatted rate requiring successive samples and represents elapsed time spent on non-idle work during the sample interval. It is not `\Process(*)\% Processor Time`, whose semantics and range differ, and not `Processor Information\% Processor Utility`, which accounts for performance state and Turbo Boost and can exceed 100. Current Task Manager can display utility; compare this UC to the exact counter in Windows Performance Monitor, not merely to the Task Manager CPU tile.

`_Total` is the host aggregate. Individual `Processor` instances (`0`, `1`, and so on) are useful drilldown data but are excluded from the primary alert. Do not sum logical-processor percentages; `_Total` is already their average. Do not divide by core count, invert `% Idle Time` without a separately tested mapping, add `% User Time` and `% Privileged Time`, or mix Processor Time with Processor Utility. The catalogue threshold is 90 percentage points, inclusive, in each of three consecutive five-minute averages. This is a 15-minute bucket-persistence policy, not a claim that every raw sample is at least 90. Microsoft describes sustained 80% or higher as a high-CPU troubleshooting scenario and 80–100 as critical guidance; 90 is a conservative deployment starting point. Tune by service class and approved objectives after baseline evidence.

Collection interval is 30 seconds. A normal complete five-minute bucket therefore has about ten samples. The SPL accepts 8 through 12 unique valid timestamps spanning at least 210 seconds, tolerating limited scheduling/index loss while rejecting sparse or implausibly dense data. That tolerance is not permission to ignore missing data: a separate health control must report every rejected sample and under-covered host. The search deliberately examines the closed interval from 25 minutes ago through 10 minutes ago, yielding exactly three aligned five-minute buckets and leaving at least ten minutes for collection/indexing. Measure actual p99 indexing delay and change the delayed window, freshness controls, tests, and operational latency together.

## Step 1 — Configure and verify the Windows Perfmon input

Create or update `%SPLUNK_HOME%\etc\apps\Splunk_TA_windows\local\inputs.conf` through a deployment app. Pin this use case to event-index `single` mode so each event has the `counter`, `instance`, and `Value` fields searched by the primary SPL:

```ini
[perfmon://CPU]
disabled = 0
object = Processor
counters = % Processor Time
instances = _Total
interval = 30
useEnglishOnly = true
mode = single
index = perfmon
```

The stanza name `CPU` establishes the expected collection/source identity used by the add-on, while `object`, `counter`, and `instance` establish the Windows PDH path. `useEnglishOnly=true` requests English object/counter names on localized Windows installations; qualify this on every supported locale. Semicolon-separated extra counters or `instances=*` can support drilldowns, but they increase volume and must not weaken the primary filters. If another deployment app already owns `[perfmon://CPU]`, merge ownership deliberately rather than defining competing stanzas. Restart or deploy according to the forwarder change procedure, then verify the winning settings on a canary:

```powershell
& "$env:SPLUNK_HOME\bin\splunk.exe" btool inputs list CPU --debug
```

Require one enabled effective stanza, the expected deployment-app path, `interval=30`, `object=Processor`, `_Total`, and the intended index/mode. Do not infer effective settings from one file. Record the forwarder GUID and canonical Splunk `host`; cloned host metadata can merge unrelated machines.

After at least two collection intervals, inspect raw events:

```spl
index=perfmon source="Perfmon:CPU" sourcetype="Perfmon:CPU" earliest=-10m
| table _time _indextime host source sourcetype collection object counter instance Value
| sort 0 host _time
```

A valid event must identify the exact object/counter/instance, contain a numeric `Value` from 0 through 100, use the intended host, and have plausible `_time` and `_indextime`. A representative `single` event contains lines equivalent to `collection=CPU`, `object=Processor`, `counter="% Processor Time"`, `instance=_Total`, and `Value=<percentage points>`. Search actual fields after every add-on upgrade; do not rely on display labels alone.

Use Windows Performance Monitor (`perfmon.exe`) on the same canary and add `Processor > % Processor Time > _Total`. Compare nearby values and trends, allowing for display and collection timing. For an exact external check, use a Windows Data Collector Set configured for that path and interval. Task Manager is only contextual because its modern CPU display can correspond to Processor Utility. Record Windows counter availability with `typeperf -qx "Processor"` or the approved PowerShell counter enumeration under the same locale.

This event implementation is intentionally distinct from two supported alternatives. `mode=multikv` produces `PerfmonMk:CPU` and different field shape; write and test a MultiKV search rather than aiming this SPL at it. A metrics index uses `mode=single` plus a metrics index and is searched with `mstats`, commonly with metric name `Processor.%_Processor_Time` and dimension `instance=_Total`; it does not produce event rows searchable by this SPL. Never dual-route both modes under one authority without duplicate and parity controls.

At 30 seconds, one `_Total` counter yields about 2,880 small events per host per day. Measure actual license bytes, index size, forwarder CPU, queueing, and search concurrency on canaries. Collecting all processor instances, all CPU counters, Process/Process V2, or one-second troubleshooting data is a separate sizing decision.

## Step 2 — Build source health before alerting

Maintain a governed lookup such as `windows_expected_hosts.csv` with exact `host`, owner, service, environment, enabled epoch, and retirement epoch. Compare it to recent valid `_Total` samples. Report expected hosts with no event after two intervals plus measured indexing delay; `_indextime-_time` above policy; wrong source/source type/object/counter/instance; nonnumeric, negative, or greater-than-100 values; duplicate `(host,_time)` rows; cadence outside the 8..12-per-five-minute envelope; sample span below 210 seconds; future timestamps; stale hosts; multiple forwarder identities for one host; and one forwarder identity producing multiple host names.

A useful health search starts with the exact primary source but does not discard malformed rows before counting them. Calculate `numeric_value=tonumber(Value)`, validity flags, `count by host,_time` for duplicates, then five-minute counts/spans. Keep wrong-counter and wrong-instance searches outside the exact primary filter so configuration drift remains visible. Alert telemetry health to the Splunk/Windows platform owner, not the application on-call. A quiet high-CPU rule is not proof of normal CPU when a host is missing or rejected.

Establish an ingestion service objective from measured delay rather than assumption. The primary closed window ends ten minutes before dispatch. If p99 indexing lag approaches that close delay, investigate forwarder output queues, receiver/indexer health, time synchronization, and event timestamping before widening the delay. Widening increases detection latency and can mask a collection defect. Preserve `_time`, `_indextime`, and effective input revision in health evidence.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the persistence search

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_cpu_utilization_trending` in a version-controlled search app. Schedule it every five minutes on aligned boundaries, for example cron `2-57/5 * * * *`, while retaining the embedded `earliest=-25m@m latest=-10m@m`. The two-minute scheduler offset reduces boundary contention; the SPL's absolute bounds remain the data contract. Configure the saved search to trigger when result count is greater than zero. Do not use real-time search for this capacity signal.

```spl
index=perfmon source="Perfmon:CPU" sourcetype="Perfmon:CPU" object="Processor" counter="% Processor Time" instance="_Total" earliest=-25m@m latest=-10m@m
| eval cpu_pct=tonumber(Value), sample_epoch=_time, valid_value=if(isnotnull(cpu_pct) AND cpu_pct>=0 AND cpu_pct<=100,1,0)
| stats count AS raw_event_count sum(valid_value) AS valid_event_count avg(cpu_pct) AS cpu_pct max(_indextime) AS last_indextime by host _time
| where raw_event_count=1 AND valid_event_count=1
| eval sample_epoch=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS sample_count avg(cpu_pct) AS avg_cpu_pct min(cpu_pct) AS min_cpu_pct max(cpu_pct) AS peak_cpu_pct min(sample_epoch) AS first_sample_epoch max(sample_epoch) AS last_sample_epoch max(last_indextime) AS last_indextime by host _time
| eval sample_span_seconds=last_sample_epoch-first_sample_epoch
| where sample_count>=8 AND sample_count<=12 AND sample_span_seconds>=210
| eval bucket_over_threshold=if(avg_cpu_pct>=90,1,0)
| stats count AS qualified_buckets sum(bucket_over_threshold) AS high_buckets sum(sample_count) AS sample_count avg(avg_cpu_pct) AS sustained_avg_cpu_pct min(min_cpu_pct) AS minimum_cpu_pct max(peak_cpu_pct) AS peak_cpu_pct min(_time) AS first_bucket_epoch max(_time) AS last_bucket_epoch max(last_indextime) AS last_indextime by host
| where qualified_buckets=3 AND high_buckets=3 AND last_bucket_epoch-first_bucket_epoch=600
| eval sustained_avg_cpu_pct=round(sustained_avg_cpu_pct,2), minimum_cpu_pct=round(minimum_cpu_pct,2), peak_cpu_pct=round(peak_cpu_pct,2), threshold_pct=90, persistence_minutes=15, recovery_pct=80, use_case="UC-1.2.1"
| table host sustained_avg_cpu_pct minimum_cpu_pct peak_cpu_pct threshold_pct persistence_minutes recovery_pct qualified_buckets high_buckets sample_count first_bucket_epoch last_bucket_epoch last_indextime use_case
| sort 0 -sustained_avg_cpu_pct host
```

The base terms enforce the event index, collection identity, Windows object, aggregate instance, and time-based counter. `tonumber` prevents lexical comparison; the validity flag rejects null and values outside the Microsoft-documented range. The first `stats` groups exact host/timestamp identity and requires one raw event, so replay duplicates cannot increase sample density or average. Near-duplicates with different timestamps require health/inventory detection.

`bin span=5m` aligns samples to stable wall-clock buckets. Bucket statistics preserve average, minimum, peak, count, first/last sample, and newest indexing time. Count and span checks require useful coverage across the bucket rather than eight samples clustered at one edge. `bucket_over_threshold` uses `>=90`, so exactly 90 qualifies and 89.99 does not. The final aggregation requires all three expected buckets to be qualified and high and verifies their starts are exactly 600 seconds apart. This prevents high/low/high, two-bucket, or gapped data from appearing persistent.

`sustained_avg_cpu_pct` is the unweighted average of three bucket averages. Because each bucket passes a bounded coverage policy, no sparse bucket can dominate; this value is for display, while `high_buckets=3` is the trigger. `minimum_cpu_pct` can be below 90 because policy applies to each bucket average, not every sample. Preserve that distinction in alert text. Peak is context, not a separate threshold.

Keep threshold, persistence, coverage, delay, and recovery in a versioned policy. If a service needs 85%, 95%, ten minutes, or 30 minutes, create a named policy revision and regression tests rather than changing numbers silently. Avoid a lookup-driven threshold until lookup schema, defaults, missing-row behavior, ownership, and change control are tested. Fleetwide one-size thresholds are a starting point, not capacity truth.

Recovery must be explicit and hysteretic. Use the same qualification pipeline over three consecutive buckets, with all three `avg_cpu_pct<80`, to close the incident. A value from 80 through less than 90 keeps an existing incident open without creating another page. Incident tooling should own state; a stateless search cannot know whether a host is already open. Throttle duplicate notification by exact `host,policy_id` for at least the evaluation period, but continue writing every evaluation result.

For dashboards, use a separate trend search over a longer time range that validates raw values and bins by host/time but does not filter to high buckets. Never use the alert's filtered rows as a complete CPU time series. Treat missing or rejected buckets as gaps, not zero.

## Step 4 — Validate source truth, SPL gates, CIM, and controls

Perform synthetic SPL testing in an isolated index with absolute `earliest`/`latest` times or a controlled fixture harness. Replace relative search bounds only in the test copy; preserve all other logic. For the positive fixture create ten unique samples in each of three consecutive five-minute buckets for `win-cpu-positive`, each bucket averaging exactly 92. Assert one row and every output named in `controlTest`. Confirm raw event count 30, accepted sample count 30, bucket starts 600 seconds apart, and rounded average 92.

Run each negative case separately so one failure cannot hide another. Assert zero primary rows for two buckets, high/low/high, 89.99, only seven samples, eight samples spanning 180 seconds, a missing middle bucket, a fourth unrelated older bucket outside the absolute window, duplicate exact timestamps, invalid strings, -0.01, 100.01, wrong host metadata, `instance=0`, `instances=*` per-core events, `Processor Information`, `% Processor Utility`, `% Idle Time`, wrong source, `PerfmonMk:CPU`, and future/stale time. Boundary fixtures must prove 90.0 qualifies, 89.99 does not, eight samples and 210 seconds qualify, seven or 209 seconds do not, 12 samples qualify, and 13 do not. Confirm a duplicate timestamp is rejected rather than averaged.

Test scheduling boundaries with samples exactly at bucket starts and just before ends. Splunk time bounds are start-inclusive and end-exclusive in normal use; verify behavior on the deployed platform with absolute epochs. Test daylight-saving transitions: `_time` is epoch-based and five-minute binning should remain continuous even when local wall time repeats or skips, but alert display must state timezone. Test host reboot and forwarder restart to ensure the first PDH rate sample and temporary gaps cannot create a complete false bucket.

On a Windows canary, generate only an approved, reversible workload. Compare the exact counter in `perfmon.exe` and indexed raw events over the same period. Do not saturate a production host merely to test. In a lab, drive a controlled CPU workload long enough for three closed buckets, then stop it and observe three qualified below-80 recovery buckets. Capture process identity, workload command, host, start/end epoch, Perfmon view, raw events, alert result, and recovery. Synthetic events prove search gates; a canary proves PDH/input behavior; neither validates production thresholds.

Validate drilldown counters without making them trigger inputs: individual `Processor` instances for imbalance, `System\Processor Queue Length`, `% User Time`, `% Privileged Time`, `% DPC Time`, and `% Interrupt Time`. For process attribution use Process or Process V2 according to supported Windows/add-on behavior and remember process percentages have different multiprocessor semantics. Microsoft recommends detailed one-to-five-second Perfmon/WPR capture during active troubleshooting; do not increase fleet baseline cadence to one second by default.

Validate CIM separately. Confirm `Perfmon:CPU` is selected by the installed add-on's event type, tagged `performance` and `cpu`, maps the exact percentage to `cpu_load_percent`, and maps host identity to `dest`. Open CIM Performance > CPU in Pivot and inspect the generated search/data before enabling acceleration. Compare raw and CIM values/host counts over fixed windows. Then run `cimSpl` with `summariesonly=t` and inspect summary coverage. Standard CIM does not retain the `_Total` identity or raw coverage contract, and it can combine other tagged CPU sources, so the CIM result is corroboration/trending only. If exact paging from acceleration is required, design a purpose-specific summary preserving source, object, counter, instance, sample identity, count/span, and rejection status; do not relabel generic CIM output as equivalent.

If using a metric index instead, discover actual names with `mcatalog`, then validate a separately saved search based on `mstats` for `metric_name="Processor.%_Processor_Time"` and `instance="_Total"`. Compare metric and event paths on a canary before migration. Disable one authority after acceptance to prevent duplicate collection and cost.

Keep `status=draft` until runtime tests, source-health coverage, alert/recovery state, dashboard, RBAC, cost, exception expiry, evidence retention, and runbook are accepted by accountable Windows and Splunk owners. Documentation review alone cannot produce `verified` status.

## Step 5 — Operationalize triage, suppression, and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`, with telemetry health first. Dashboard viewers need only read access to the approved index and app; raw-event access may reveal infrastructure naming and workload patterns, so scope roles appropriately. Show UTC or label local timezone. For 24-hour operations display five-minute averages and coverage. For capacity review add daily p50/p95/maximum and hours above policy, but recompute from qualified buckets; do not average host averages into a fleet percentage without weighting and a clear question.

Alert title should state: `Windows aggregate Processor Time >=90% in 3 consecutive qualified 5m buckets: $result.host$`. Include sustained average, minimum, peak, sample count, bucket epochs in human-readable UTC, dashboard link, telemetry-health status, service owner, policy revision, and runbook. Route warning or ticket severity according to service objectives; escalate when latency/errors, failover risk, or repeated recurrence corroborates impact. CPU percentage alone does not determine incident severity.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify three qualified consecutive buckets, exact `_Total` counter, valid source health, host identity, no duplicate collector, and no active bounded exception.
2. Compare the same counter in Perfmon and inspect individual processor instances. Note whether pressure is balanced or affinity-bound.
3. Correlate application latency, errors, request rate, queues, service health, load-balancer membership, and peer capacity. High CPU without impact can be efficient utilization; impact at lower CPU can indicate another bottleneck.
4. Split time into `% User Time`, `% Privileged Time`, `% DPC Time`, and `% Interrupt Time`; inspect `System\Processor Queue Length` with processor count and workload context. Do not diagnose solely from queue length.
5. Identify processes with Task Manager, Resource Monitor, Process Explorer, or qualified Process/Process V2 telemetry. During active high CPU, follow Microsoft guidance for a short Perfmon log, WPR CPU profile, and approved dump/trace collection. Those tools may collect sensitive process and stack information; follow incident and privacy controls.
6. Correlate Windows Update, Defender/EDR, backup, inventory, vulnerability scanning, deployments, failover, batch schedules, hypervisor contention, and power plan.
7. Choose an owner and safe action: workload tune, schedule change, scale-out/up, affinity correction, driver/security-agent investigation, vendor escalation, or approved restart/failover. Preserve before/after data.

Never automatically kill a process, restart a service or host, change affinity, disable security software, change a power plan, add CPUs, migrate a VM, or capture a dump from this result alone. Those actions can interrupt service, destroy evidence, expose data, or shift load. Require service-specific authorization and verify recovery with application objectives and three qualified below-80 buckets—not merely one low sample.

For approved load tests and maintenance, apply `windows_cpu_exceptions.csv` only after the base result. Require exact host and policy ID, numeric start/end epochs, owner, approver, ticket, reason, and finite expiry. Validate `valid_from_epoch<=evaluation_epoch<valid_until_epoch`. Reject wildcard hosts, broad environment rows, absent dates, text dates without parsing tests, and exceptions that suppress source health. Keep suppressed detections in an audit destination and report exceptions approaching expiry. A test should prove one named host is notification-suppressed only during its window while another host still pages.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` according to local operational policy. The 30-day raw retention in `cost` is an advisory estimate, not a compliance requirement. Hash/version search and configuration exports where local evidence processes require integrity. Every result should be reproducible from retained raw samples or a governed summary that preserves the same contract.

Review quarterly and after Windows feature updates, processor/hypervisor changes, add-on/forwarder/CIM upgrades, input-mode changes, index migrations, host naming changes, scheduler changes, or major workload shifts. Rebaseline by service class; keep a dated approval explaining why 90/15/80 remains appropriate.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot by preserving the measurement contract

- **No `Perfmon:CPU` events:** verify forwarder service and deployment-client status, app assignment, effective `[perfmon://CPU]` stanza, index existence/permissions, outputs/queues, receiver path, and `splunkd.log` messages from the Perfmon input. Confirm `disabled=0`. Do not substitute WMI or Task Manager data under the same source type.
- **Input reports object/counter not found:** enumerate the local performance library and verify locale. Keep `useEnglishOnly=true` if qualified; otherwise use a separately tested localized stanza/source contract. Repair Windows performance counters only under Microsoft procedure and change control.
- **First sample missing after restart:** PDH rate counters require successive collections. A startup gap is expected but must remain visible to source health; the 8-sample/210-second gate prevents one startup value from qualifying a bucket.
- **Events are `PerfmonMk:CPU`:** effective `mode=multikv` differs from this implementation. Either pin `mode=single` for event data or build/test a MultiKV search using its actual field extraction. Do not add both source types to an `OR` clause without normalizing and duplicate testing.
- **Data is in a metrics index:** event search returning nothing is expected. Use `mcatalog` and a separately validated `mstats` search for the actual metric/dimensions, or route this dedicated source to an event index. Never use normal index search as proof that metrics are absent.
- **`Value` is null or text:** inspect `_raw`, sourcetype, add-on knowledge placement, field permissions, mode, and upgrade notes. Do not coalesce null to zero; null is unknown and belongs in source health.
- **Values exceed 100:** verify the exact object/counter. Processor Utility and Process counters have different ranges. For this `Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` contract, preserve the raw event as a defect and reject it; do not cap with `min(value,100)`.
- **Task Manager disagrees:** add the exact Processor Time counter in Perfmon. Task Manager can show frequency-adjusted Processor Utility, and sampling windows differ. Check throttling/Turbo Boost and timestamps; do not tune this threshold to force visual equality.
- **Duplicate or over-dense samples:** inspect duplicate `[perfmon://CPU]` definitions, deployment-app precedence, cloned forwarder/host identities, replay routes, and dual collection. Exact timestamp duplicates are rejected; near-duplicates require cadence health. Fix authority rather than deduplicating arbitrary values.
- **Sparse bucket or long indexing delay:** inspect forwarder CPU/output queues, network, receiver/indexer health, blocked queues, clock sync, and `_indextime-_time`. Do not lower the eight-sample or 210-second gate merely to recover alert rows.
- **High raw trend but no alert:** inspect each of the three bucket averages, counts, spans, exact bucket starts, validity, and search bounds. One bucket below 90, under-covered, or nonconsecutive correctly prevents firing. Minimum sample can be below 90 while average qualifies.
- **Alert repeats continuously:** verify incident-key throttling by exact host/policy, state integration, and recovery search. Do not permanently suppress the host; retain evaluations and use 80-percent hysteresis.
- **CIM search is empty:** verify tags/aliases, `dest`, `cpu_load_percent`, model acceleration, summary range/completion, app context, and search permissions. `summariesonly=t` intentionally excludes raw fallback. Keep raw event search authoritative.
- **CIM differs from raw:** identify other tagged CPU sources, missing `_Total` semantics, destination mapping, acceleration lag, field-unit changes, or mixed instances. Standard CIM is not exact-source evidence; do not average the discrepancy away.
- **One core saturated but aggregate below 90:** this UC correctly does not fire. Use per-core analysis and service-latency policy; do not reinterpret `_Total` as worst-core usage.
- **Aggregate high but service healthy:** verify authorized workload and headroom/failover objectives. Route to capacity review or bounded suppression when policy permits, while retaining the real signal.
- **Host reboot or clock change creates gaps:** correlate boot/service events, Windows Time, `_time`, `_indextime`, and schedule. Never use `abs(now()-_time)` or fill gaps with zero; repair time/collection and preserve unknown periods.
grandmaExplanation: We watch how busy each Windows server stays and wait for several complete checks before warning anyone. That helps the team investigate computers that may be running out of breathing room without overreacting to a brief burst of work.
